title: Maybe, Probably, Possibly
theme: Uncertainty and probability: degrees of knowing
objectives: I can describe how sure I am using words such as probable, plausible, tentative, and inconclusive.
I can tell surmise, presume, assume, and conjecture apart by how much evidence stands behind the guess.
I can write a short explanation that separates what is known from what is only supposed.
I can use the prefixes in- and un- and the endings -able, -ible, and -ive to understand describing words.
rationale: Scientists and historians rarely know for sure, and students who can only say yes or no cannot read their reports. This unit gives a ladder of certainty (inconclusive, tentative, plausible, probable) and the verbs of educated guessing (surmise, presume, assume), with conjecture and hypothetical for the ideas that come out of them and unforeseen for what no one predicted. Presume and assume are flagged as confusable because students use them interchangeably; the unit asks them to say how much evidence is behind a statement. Inference, deduce, verify, and quantify return from the analysis and data units as the tools that move a guess toward knowledge.

words.def: Likely to happen or to be true, though not certain.
words.ex: With dark clouds overhead, rain is probable this afternoon.
words.ex2: It is probable that the experiment will fail if the temperature is not kept steady.
words.nonExample: An event that cannot possibly happen is not probable.

apps.academic: In math, the probability of an event tells how probable it is, from zero to one.
apps.spoken: It's probable that we'll be late, so let's text them.
apps.writing: Use probable when the evidence makes something likely but not certain.

cloze.s: Because the road was covered in ice, a delay in the bus schedule was ___.

cloze2.s: Scientists said it was ___ that the new drug would work, but they wanted more tests before they were sure.

misuse.s: It is probable that the sun will rise in the west tomorrow morning.
misuse.why: Probable means likely; the sun rising in the west will not happen.

words.def: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true, even if not proven.
words.ex: Her excuse sounded plausible, since the bus really had been late that morning.
words.ex2: A plausible theory must fit all of the facts we have collected so far.
words.nonExample: A story about a dog that drives a school bus is not plausible.

apps.academic: A plausible explanation is one that fits the evidence, but it still needs testing.
apps.spoken: That's plausible, but how could we check it?
apps.writing: Use plausible for an explanation that is believable; use probable for something likely.

cloze.s: The jury found his story ___, since every detail matched the security video.

cloze2.s: Only a ___ theory can fit all of the footprints, the broken fence, and the missing beans.

misuse.s: The plausible explanation was a wild tale that contradicted every fact we had collected.
misuse.why: Plausible means reasonable and believable; a tale that contradicts every fact is not.

visual.alt: A face with a monocle beside a light bulb.

words.def: To guess that something is true based on limited evidence.
words.ex: From the muddy boots by the door, I surmised that my brother had been hiking.
words.ex2: The archaeologists surmised that the room had been a kitchen because they found a hearth and clay pots.
words.nonExample: Knowing the answer for certain from a signed confession is not surmising.

apps.academic: Historians surmise how people lived from the few objects that survive.
apps.spoken: I surmise that they're running late, since no one has arrived.
apps.writing: Use surmise when a writer guesses from a few clues, not from complete proof.

cloze.s: Seeing the umbrella dripping by the door, she could ___ that it had started to rain.

cloze2.s: We can only ___ what the writer meant, since half of the letter is torn away.

misuse.s: He surmised the answer with complete certainty after reading the signed confession.
misuse.why: To surmise is to guess from limited evidence; a signed confession gives certainty.

visual.alt: A detective with a thought bubble.

words.def: Based on an imagined situation or a possible idea, not a real one.
words.ex: The teacher asked a hypothetical question: what would happen if the moon disappeared tomorrow?
words.ex2: Hypothetical examples help students test an idea before they try it for real.
words.nonExample: A temperature recorded on a real thermometer is not hypothetical.

apps.academic: A hypothetical situation lets you test an idea without real consequences.
apps.spoken: Hypothetically, what if we skipped lunch and went straight to the game?
apps.writing: Use hypothetical for an imagined case that is used to test or explain an idea.

cloze.s: The lawyer posed a ___ situation: what if the contract had been signed a day earlier?

cloze2.s: Because the plan was only ___, no money had actually been spent.

misuse.s: The hypothetical meal was real, hot, and eaten by everyone at the table.
misuse.why: Hypothetical means imagined; a real, eaten meal is not hypothetical.

visual.alt: A thought bubble above a crescent moon.

words.def: Not final or certain; open to change.
words.ex: We made tentative plans for the picnic, depending on the weather.
words.ex2: Her tentative answer showed that she was still thinking the question through.
words.nonExample: A final decision signed by everyone is not tentative.

apps.academic: A tentative conclusion says what the data suggest and admits what is not yet known.
apps.spoken: It's only a tentative date, so don't book anything yet.
apps.writing: Use tentative for conclusions or plans that may change with new information.

cloze.s: The scientists announced a ___ result, saying that more tests were needed before they could be sure.

cloze2.s: Our ___ schedule might change, so please check it again on Friday.

misuse.s: The tentative decision was final and could never be changed for any reason.
misuse.why: Tentative means not final and open to change; a decision that can never change is the opposite.

visual.alt: A pencil beside a question mark.

words.frame: Our tentative plan is ___, but it could change if ___.

words.def: To suppose that something is true because it is likely, without having proof.
words.ex: I presume you have already eaten, since it is past nine o'clock.
words.ex2: In court, a person is presumed innocent until the evidence proves otherwise.
words.nonExample: Checking the records to find out for sure is not presuming.

apps.academic: Historians presume that a letter is genuine until they find evidence that it is not.
apps.spoken: I presume you're coming; the invitation was for everyone.
apps.writing: Use presume when there is a good reason to think something is true but no proof.

cloze.s: When she did not answer the phone during the day, I ___ that she was in a meeting.

cloze2.s: Unless someone proves otherwise, we ___ that the bridge is safe, since it passed its inspection last week.

misuse.s: I presume it is true because I have checked every record and seen the proof myself.
misuse.why: To presume is to suppose without proof; having checked every record means you know.

visual.alt: A shrugging person beside a clipboard.

words.def: To accept something as true without checking it first.

senses.def: To take on a role or a responsibility.
senses.example: She assumed the role of team captain when the old captain moved away.

words.ex: Don't assume the store is open on a holiday; call first.
words.ex2: Many people assume that heavier objects fall faster, but careful tests show otherwise.
words.nonExample: Testing an idea and finding proof is not assuming it.

apps.academic: An assumption is an idea you accept as true while you work out the rest of a problem.
apps.spoken: Don't assume I know what you mean; explain it again.
apps.writing: Use assume when a person accepts something without checking, which can lead to errors.

cloze.s: It is risky to ___ that your answer is right without double-checking the calculation.

cloze2.s: Never ___ that a website is accurate just because it looks professional.

misuse.s: She assumed the claim was true by checking every fact and reading three sources.
misuse.why: To assume is to accept something without checking; checking every fact is the opposite.

visual.alt: A warning sign beside a thinking face.

words.def: A guess based on some evidence but not enough to prove it.
words.ex: Her conjecture was that the missing keys were in the car, but she had not looked yet.
words.ex2: In math, a conjecture is an idea that seems true but has not yet been proven.
words.nonExample: A fact confirmed by three experiments is no longer a conjecture.

apps.academic: A conjecture becomes a conclusion only after it is tested and supported.
apps.spoken: That's just a conjecture; we don't have proof yet.
apps.writing: Use conjecture for an unproven idea that is based on some evidence.

cloze.s: Without any footprints or photos, the explanation was pure ___, not proven fact.

cloze2.s: The mathematician wrote down a ___ about prime numbers and spent years trying to prove it.

misuse.s: A conjecture is a fact so firmly proven that no one can question it.
misuse.why: A conjecture is an unproven guess, not a proven fact.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass beside a question mark.

words.frame: My conjecture is that ___, but I need to ___.

words.def: Not leading to a clear answer or a final decision.
words.ex: The first test was inconclusive, so the team repeated it with a larger sample.
words.ex2: After three hours of talk, the meeting was inconclusive, and nothing was decided.
words.nonExample: A test that clearly proves the answer is not inconclusive.

apps.academic: Inconclusive results mean the data do not support a clear conclusion.
apps.spoken: The talks were inconclusive, so they will meet again.
apps.writing: Use inconclusive for evidence or results that do not settle the question.

cloze.s: The detective said the evidence was ___, so no one could be charged yet.

cloze2.s: Because the results were ___, the scientists planned a second experiment.

misuse.s: The inconclusive test gave a clear, final answer that settled the question forever.
misuse.why: Inconclusive means no clear answer; a clear, final answer is the opposite.

visual.alt: A test tube beside a question mark.

words.def: Not expected or predicted; happening without warning.
words.ex: An unforeseen delay kept the train in the station for two hours.
words.ex2: The team's plan failed because of an unforeseen change in the weather.
words.nonExample: A holiday that appears on the calendar every year is not unforeseen.

segs.m: known or seen ahead of time

apps.academic: Scientists record unforeseen results because they may lead to new questions.
apps.spoken: We had an unforeseen problem with the bus.
apps.writing: Use unforeseen for an event nobody predicted, not for one that was merely unwanted.

cloze.s: Because of an ___ power outage, the concert began an hour late.

cloze2.s: Even the best planners cannot prepare for every ___ problem that might appear.

misuse.s: The unforeseen storm had been predicted by every forecaster for an entire week.
misuse.why: Unforeseen means not expected; a storm predicted for a week was expected.

passage.title: Who Ate the Beans?
paras: On Monday morning, the school garden looked as if a storm had passed through it. Half of the bean plants were missing, and the soil was dotted with small holes. Ms. Alvarado gathered her science club by the fence. "Before anyone names a culprit," she said, "let's separate what we know from what we only presume."

Jonah spoke first. "It was deer," he announced. "I assume deer eat beans." Ms. Alvarado asked him to turn his idea into a hypothesis, and after a moment Jonah wrote, "If deer ate the beans, there will be hoofprints." Mina raised her hand. "Let's ask a hypothetical question," she said. "If a rabbit had done it, what would we see that is different?"

The club measured the holes and searched for tracks. Small prints near the fence made a rabbit plausible, since they were only an inch wide, but a deer was still possible if it had leaned over the fence. Priya made a tentative list: "Rabbit, probable. Deer, possible. Squirrel, unlikely." Ms. Alvarado liked the word tentative. "A tentative answer is one we are ready to change," she said.

Then came an unforeseen problem. That night a heavy rain washed away every track. On Tuesday the club had only a few photographs and the holes, and the evidence was inconclusive. "We cannot even surmise what happened," Jonah complained. Mina disagreed. "We can. The holes are small, the prints are small, and the stems were chewed low to the ground. That points to a small animal."

The club still wrote a conjecture on the board: a rabbit ate the beans, probably from the east side. Then they set up a camera by the fence to test it. "Science is not about being certain right away," Ms. Alvarado said. "It is about being careful about how certain you are." Two nights later, a rabbit hopped into the camera's view and nibbled a bean leaf. Jonah grinned and erased his hasty guess.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "tentative" most nearly means
qs.why: Ms. Alvarado explains that a tentative answer is one we are ready to change.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Alvarado ask Jonah to turn his idea into a hypothesis?
choices: She wants him to stop talking.
She wants an idea that can be tested instead of just believed.
She thinks deer are not a possible cause.
She wants the club to give up on the garden.
qs.why: Her "If deer ate the beans, there will be hoofprints" format makes an idea that can be checked.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the evidence was inconclusive on Tuesday?
choices: A rabbit nibbled a bean leaf.
The club set up a camera by the fence.
The rain washed away every track, leaving only a few photographs and the holes.
qs.why: With the tracks gone, the club could not point to a single clear answer.

qs.q: When Jonah says "I assume deer eat beans," he is
choices: proving a fact with a measurement
accepting an idea as true without checking it
repeating a conclusion from the camera
qs.why: He states an idea without any test or evidence, which is what assume means.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Deer are the main cause of garden damage.
A good scientist matches how sure she is to the evidence she has.
qs.why: Ms. Alvarado says the goal is to be careful about how certain you are, and the club tests rather than assumes.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for talking about degrees of certainty, read a narrative about a school-garden mystery, practice prefixes and endings, and write short explanations that separate what is known from what is supposed. The unit supports science and history writing, where a precise word for how sure the writer is matters.

notes.va.probable.adj: Link to probability in math (zero to one). Keep a number line on the board: impossible, unlikely, possible, probable, certain. Probable means more likely than not; students often use it for anything possible.
notes.va.plausible.adj: Confusable with probable. Plausible is about whether an explanation seems reasonable; probable is about how likely an event is. An explanation can be plausible and still wrong. Use a mystery and ask which explanations are plausible.
notes.va.surmise.v: A formal verb; model it with a clue (a wet umbrella) and the guess it supports. Students often say guess; ask them to name the clue that supports the guess.
notes.va.hypothetical.adj: Link to hypothesis. A hypothetical situation is imagined and used for testing an idea; a hypothesis is a testable prediction. Use 'what if' questions. Teach the word family hypothesize and hypothetically.
notes.va.tentative.adj: A key word for scientific writing. Show how tentative words (may, suggests, appears) signal openness. Ask students to rewrite a bold claim as a tentative one.
notes.va.presume.v: Confusable with assume. Presume has a good reason behind it (it is likely) and is used in law (presumed innocent). Contrast with assume, which has no check. Use a short evidence ladder to show the difference.
notes.va.assume.v: Two senses: accept without checking (taught) and take on a role (assume leadership). Keep to the first sense in practice. Link to the cost of assuming: ask what could go wrong.
notes.va.conjecture.n: A noun for an unproven idea; contrast with hypothesis (which is stated so that it can be tested) and with fact. In math, conjecture has a special sense; keep the examples general.
notes.va.inconclusive.adj: In- (not) plus conclusive. Ask students to say what data would make a result conclusive. Pair with tentative to show that an inconclusive result leads to a tentative conclusion or more testing.
notes.va.unforeseen.adj: Un- (not) plus foreseen. Distinguish from unexpected: foreseen includes foresee, so the word ties to prediction. Ask what a planner could do to prepare for unforeseen problems.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Jonah says he assumes deer eat beans. He has no evidence yet, so he is accepting something without checking. When Mina says a rabbit is plausible because the prints are small, she is using a clue. When the rain washes away the tracks, the evidence is inconclusive, so any answer must stay tentative.'
discuss: What is the difference between being sure and being right?
When is it fine to assume something, and when is it risky?
misconceptions: Presume and assume mean exactly the same thing.
A hypothesis is the same as a fact.
extend: Rewrite three bold claims from a newspaper or textbook using tentative or probable.
Design a short experiment in class, write a hypothesis, collect data, and report the result as conclusive or inconclusive.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit presume/assume and probable/plausible as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week. Ask students to apply inference, deduce, verify, and quantify to a short mystery: what can we deduce, how could we verify it, and what could we quantify.

wida.oral: Partner A shares a short claim; Partner B says how sure the claim sounds (probable, plausible, tentative, or inconclusive) and what evidence would make it more certain.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (conjeturar, suponer, asumir, provisional, no concluyente, imprevisto) not reviewed by a native speaker; check asumir against suponer for presume and assume, and whether no concluyente is idiomatic.

Sense boundaries: presume and assume overlap in everyday use; the unit treats presume as supposing from likelihood and assume as accepting without checking. Assume also has a second sense (take on a role).
Fact claims: heavier objects fall at the same rate when air resistance is negligible; a person is presumed innocent until proven otherwise in court. Confirm wording.
